Name: subliminal_statistical_signature
Title: The Trait Is in the Numbers: Decoding Subliminal Signals from the Distributional Statistics of Trait-Free Data
Short Hypothesis: The hidden trait a teacher transmits through 'semantically unrelated' number sequences is imprinted as a trait-specific, decodable signature in the low-level distributional statistics of the data (digit/leading-digit frequencies, value distribution, n-gram/positional patterns, entropy) rather than only in rare per-token divergences. We rank three claims by importance: (PRIMARY) a purely data-level, trait-agnostic Distribution-Matching Resampling defense that erases the signature and causally suppresses transmission with no model access; (SECONDARY) that student transmission strength correlates with the magnitude of this statistical signature beyond what divergence-token frequency alone explains; and (SUPPORTING) that a lightweight statistical classifier can recover which trait a teacher had from the data alone. We present the statistical-signature account as a competing explanatory hypothesis - a data-side observable of the transmission process - not an established mechanism.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate, but analyzed transmission only through the student and treated the number data as 'semantically unrelated,' never characterizing its statistical structure. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers - a per-token, model-relative account requiring a contrasting teacher to identify carrier tokens; it did not ask whether the trait is legible in the data's aggregate distributional statistics without any model. Benford's Curse (2025) shows LLMs internalize corpus digit distributions in FFN neurons that propagate to outputs, but never connects this to subliminal trait transmission. Informal speculation that teacher 'fingerprints' exist has not been operationalized: no prior work has shown (a) recovery of the specific trait from data statistics alone, (b) a quantitative linkage between signature magnitude and behavioral transmission strength B that survives controlling for divergence-token frequency, or (c) causal suppression of transmission by targeted erasure of the measured signature. This proposal is the first data-side account and is deployable by exactly the party who most needs it - a distillation consumer who receives only synthetic data and has no access to the teacher model - running a cheap statistical audit and a model-free resampling defense at the data-ingestion stage. It is distinguished from the token-level, model-relative divergence-token account (which needs a contrasting teacher and the student) and from our model-centric proposals.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through data that appears semantically unrelated to the trait - most strikingly, lists of numbers - even after every reference to the trait is filtered out. Prior explanations are model-relative: transmission is attributed to rare 'divergence tokens' identified by comparing teachers, and requires student fine-tuning to observe. We ask a purely data-side question with a directly deployable payoff for distillation consumers who receive only synthetic data: is the trait legible in the distributional statistics of the numbers themselves, and can erasing those statistics stop transmission without any model access? Our primary contribution is Distribution-Matching Resampling, a trait-agnostic, model-free defense that reweights data so its low-level feature distribution matches a no-trait control, which we test causally against untargeted perturbations of equal strength. We hypothesize trait-conditioned teachers systematically warp low-level statistics - digit/leading-digit frequencies, value magnitudes, positional and n-gram patterns, entropy - leaving a fingerprint. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) and affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we (1) train lightweight classifiers to recover the trait from data statistics, benchmarked against divergence-token-only, raw-n-gram, and teacher-ID baselines; (2) test whether signature magnitude predicts transmission strength B after partialling out divergence-token frequency, with a pre-registered power analysis; and (3) show targeted signature removal suppresses transmission more than equally strong untargeted perturbation, tracing a suppression-utility frontier. We present the statistical signature as a competing explanatory hypothesis and a deployable audit, whichever way the mechanism question resolves.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Teachers are Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B prompted to hold a trait; carriers follow the Cloud et al. number-continuation protocol (generate 30,000 completions per condition, filter to remove any trait-name/explicit content, keep and fix 10,000 per condition), with format normalization (fixed delimiter/length distribution across conditions) and deduplication, and stratified splits by teacher and generation batch so no sequence or batch is shared between train and test. Traits: 3 benign preferences (owl, a named tree, a named color), 2 safety-relevant (mild misalignment, sycophancy), plus a no-trait control; we also add style/temperature-matched teacher variants and a random-trait-relabeling control to separate trait from teacher identity. Students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP adapters, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, 3 epochs, seeds {0,1,2}). Behavioral trait strength B = held-out elicitation rate (100 probes x 20 samples, fixed-rubric judge) minus the no-trait control, in pp; mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Indecision band: classifier accuracy within +/-2 x chance-SD of chance, or |B| < 3 pp, is null.

Experiment 1 (H-supporting - the trait leaves a decodable low-level statistical signature, vs. baselines): Compute a fixed model-free feature battery (~40 features: digit frequency, leading-digit/Benford distribution, value-magnitude histogram, length/delimiter patterns, adjacent-number transition/n-gram stats, positional value distributions, per-sequence entropy, repetition rate). Train L2 logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees to predict the teacher's trait on a batch-level split. Baselines it must beat or match: (i) a raw-token n-gram classifier, (ii) a divergence-token-frequency-only predictor, and (iii) a teacher-ID classifier (to show trait, not teacher identity, is decoded - tested by predicting trait across held-out teachers). Decisive metric: held-out multi-class accuracy and per-trait AUC vs. chance and vs. baselines. Convincing: signature classifier >= 2x chance with CI excluding chance AND exceeds the divergence-token-only baseline; teacher-ID leakage controlled (trait decodable across unseen teachers). Chance-level accuracy favors the token-level account (a clean negative). The signal must survive within-sequence shuffling but be destroyed by marginal resampling.

Experiment 2 (H-supporting - distributional, not leaked content): Re-run the decoder on (a) within-sequence-shuffled and (b) marginal-resampled data. Convincing: accuracy preserved (within 3 pp) under shuffling but collapses to chance under marginal resampling. The reverse indicates order-carried or leaked-content signal.

Experiment 3 (H-secondary - transmission tracks signature strength beyond divergence tokens; pre-registered): PRE-REGISTERED analysis: >=24 teachers (traits x model x style variants), signature-strength = KL(teacher feature distribution || control) and decoder confidence margin; regress behavioral B on signature-strength. Power: with 24 teachers we can detect R^2 >= 0.3 at alpha 0.05 with power ~0.8 (reported a priori). Decisive metric: R^2 and slope. Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3, positive slope, CI excluding 0.

Experiment 4 (H-secondary - distributional vs. divergence-token carriage): Using a contrasting-base oracle (measurement only), compute the partial correlation between signature-strength and B controlling for divergence-token frequency (and vice versa), covariates pre-registered. Confirmation of an independent macroscopic contribution: signature-strength retains |partial r| >= 0.3 after controlling for divergence tokens. |partial r| < 0.1 means the fingerprint is a shadow of divergence tokens; [0.1,0.3] is inconclusive and reported as such.

Experiment 5 (H-PRIMARY - targeted resampling suppresses transmission, causally and model-free): Importance-resample each teacher's 10,000 sequences so its feature battery matches the no-trait control (no model access). Retrain matched-base students and measure residual B and utility (MMLU; HumanEval pass@1 for the code carrier). CAUSAL control: compare targeted signature-matching against an untargeted perturbation of EQUAL statistical magnitude (same total change in feature distribution applied to random directions) and against random/histogram-matching ablations and a paraphrase baseline. Decisive metric: suppression ratio 1 - B_resampled/B_original on a suppression-utility frontier, and targeted-minus-untargeted suppression. Convincing: targeted resampling gives >=50% suppression of an unsafe trait with <=2 pp utility loss AND suppresses >=10 pp more than the equal-magnitude untargeted perturbation (establishing that removing the measured signature - not generic noise - is what stops transmission). Suppression within the null band means the defense does not work; a large utility drop marks it impractical.

Experiment 6 (controls and carrier generalization): (a) matched-base gate - transmission collapses to null for mismatched-base students while the data signature remains decodable regardless of student, proving the signature is a property of generation not the student; (b) replicate decoding and the resampling defense on a code carrier; (c) verify each teacher's overt trait strength before generation and discard traits with teacher separation < 10 pp.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The trait may NOT leave a decodable aggregate fingerprint (decoding at chance), a clean negative strengthening the token-level account - still a useful clarification. 2) A decodable signature could be residual filtered-through content rather than distributional warping; we audit leakage and require the signal to survive within-sequence shuffling but be destroyed by marginal resampling, and add style/temperature-matched and random-relabel controls to separate trait from teacher identity. 3) Signature-strength and transmission could be only weakly correlated if rare tokens dominate; the pre-registered divergence-token partial-correlation (with a stated power analysis) disentangles these, and either outcome is publishable. 4) Distribution-Matching Resampling could harm utility if useful structure is entangled with the signature; we quantify the suppression-utility frontier and, critically, compare against an equal-magnitude untargeted perturbation so the causal claim is that targeted removal - not generic noise - suppresses transmission. 5) Decodable statistics may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant traits, and both number and code carriers, reporting per-family results. 6) System-prompt-induced traits may be weak; we verify teacher trait strength before generation and discard poorly separated traits.
